_comment: Sensors with no machine-readable feed. Updated by research, not by fetch.py. Each carries its own 'asof' date; the dashboard marks anything older than 45 days as stale so a forgotten sensor cannot quietly pass for a current reading. state: 0 calm, 1 watch, 2 turning.

A4.value: Meta raises the floor, Huang: demand 'off the charts'
A4.detail: The first Q3 call is in and still contains no cautious language. Meta (2026-10-21) narrowed its 2026 capex range upward to $135-145bn from $130-145bn, spent $34.9bn in the quarter and went to negative free cash flow (about -$2.1bn), saying it is still building the 2027 plan and will keep funding AI capacity; more detail comes on the Q4 call. Nvidia's Huang (GTC Berlin, 2026-10-22) called neocloud demand 'off the charts' and said the constraint is capital, not customers. That is the most important new nuance here: it is not 'digesting' language, but it names financing as the bottleneck, which is a C-cluster problem, not an A-cluster one. Oracle (2026-09-10) still holds $90-95bn for its fiscal year. Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon have not reported Q3 yet; they are the real test, and the stock-market selloff of the week of 2026-10-19 does not count under the 'no share prices' rule.
A4.source: Meta Q3 2026 release and call (2026-10-21); CNBC interview with Jensen Huang (2026-10-22); Oracle FY2027 Q1 (2026-09-10)

B2.detail: The H1 2026 surveys published in September are still the latest: CBRE primary-market vacancy a record 1.4% (Northern Virginia 0.2%), JLL North America about 1% for the third year running, 25 GW absorbed in H1 and most tenants now contracting for 2028 deliveries. JLL counts 66 GW under construction, 95% pre-committed. Nothing points to space coming free; the next reading is the year-end round in February and March.
B2.source: CBRE North America Data Center Trends H1 2026 (2026-09-08); JLL North America Data Center Report midyear 2026

B3.value: record build, cancellations doubling, for local reasons
B3.detail: Construction is still at a record — CBRE 7,481 MW under way in the primary markets, +24.8% in H1. The cancellation half keeps clustering: Uptime Institute counts 26 cancelled giant campuses in H1 2026 against 12 in all of 2025, Data Center Watch 45 US projects worth about $68bn blocked or delayed in Q2 after about $130bn in Q1, and New York stopped taking proposals for large new facilities in July. Rule 05 holds: the stated reasons are local opposition, power and permits, not tenants walking away. Watch, not turning, because construction is rising, not down 15%.
B3.source: CBRE H1 2026; Uptime Institute Update 528 (September 2026); Data Center Watch Q2 2026; Heatmap cancellation tracking

C1.value: lenders push back on the most-indebted builders
C1.detail: The volume has kept rising: Barclays counts $346bn of capital raised by hyperscalers, data-centre operators and neoclouds so far in 2026, against $172bn for all of 2025. The new part is the lender side, which since mid-October has started to refuse the weakest borrowers. CoreWeave's five-year CDS went above 1,100bp (CNBC, 2026-10-15) and its unsecured bonds yield about 15%; Oracle's spread was 308bp on 2026-10-21 against 141bp on 2026-01-02; SoftBank's CDS is near a four-year high above 420bp; Meta's CDS is reported at a record of about 115bp; a Korean neocloud IPO failed (PitchBook). Evercore's desk sums up the market's line as no more AI debt without operating cash flow behind it, and Huang publicly called capital 'scarce'. Still watch, not turning: the turn needs most new spending to be borrowed, and the five large buyers still pay most of it from cash (see A2). But this is the sensor closest to turning, and the stress sits exactly where the thesis expects it: with the companies that build on borrowed money rather than with the cash-rich hyperscalers. C2 cannot see this, because it measures the whole high-yield market.
C1.source: CNBC on CoreWeave CDS (2026-10-15) and Oracle spreads (2026-10-21/22); Barclays research via Yahoo Finance (October 2026); PitchBook on the Korean neocloud IPO; CNBC Huang interview (2026-10-22)

C3.value: no new change; Microsoft's 25-year buildings now in force
C3.detail: No filer has changed server lives or written down AI equipment since September. The standing picture: Microsoft's longer life for data centres and office buildings (15 to 25 years) applies from FY2027, which began in July, so its first effect shows in the late-October results. Amazon remains the one company to have shortened (a subset of servers, six to five years), Meta the one to have stretched (5.5 years). The 10-Qs due in late October and early November are the next check.
C3.source: 10-K and 10-Q useful-life disclosures; Microsoft FY2026 Q4 disclosure

C4.value: $308bn, $212bn, $159bn: two falls, both from the two labs
C4.detail: Global venture funding fell for a second quarter, to $159bn in Q3 from $212bn in Q2 and $308bn in Q1 (Crunchbase), which meets the letter of the turn. Read as the sensor's note asks, it does not meet the substance: Q1 held $188bn in four rounds (OpenAI $122bn, Anthropic $30bn, xAI $20bn, Waymo $16bn), and without OpenAI and Anthropic the quarters run roughly $156bn, $147bn, $159bn — flat to up. Q3 was +53% year on year, AI took $102bn (64%), and a record 27 companies raised $1bn or more. No reporting of ratchets, preference stacks or down rounds at the large labs. Raised to watch because the headline now falls and the next lab round decides the direction; scored turning only if amounts fall without the mega-round explanation or terms harden. Update 2026-10-23: no new quarterly figure (Q4 data comes in early January), but the terms side is hardening at the edge: a Korean neocloud IPO failed in October and Huang called capital 'scarce' for neoclouds. These are public markets and credit, not venture rounds, so they do not move the sensor yet; the next lab round decides.
C4.source: Crunchbase News Q3 2026 global funding report (early October 2026); Crunchbase Q1 and H1 2026 data; PitchBook (October 2026); CNBC Huang interview (2026-10-22)

D1.detail: The turn the September reading expected has come. Smartphones fell 6.7% in Q2 (IDC) and about 20% in Q3 (Counterpoint, preliminary; the lowest third quarter since 2012) — two quarters beyond -5%. PCs fell 20.1% to 62.7m in Q3 after a revised -3.8% in Q2 (IDC). China alone fell 15.4%, its sixth straight decline. Every source names the same cause: memory and component costs pushing up shelf prices. The caveat for PCs is real — IDC says buyers stocked up early in the year ahead of price rises, borrowing from H2 — but the phone decline has no such pull-in behind it, and IDC expects the next few quarters to get worse before they improve. IDC's own global phone figure for Q3 is still due.
D1.source: IDC PC tracker Q3 2026 (2026-10-08); IDC China smartphone Q3 2026 (2026-10-13); Counterpoint global smartphone Q3 2026 preliminary; IDC Q2 2026

D4.value: AI seats and ARR still expanding
D4.detail: The large sellers still report expansion, not cancellation. Salesforce (Q2 FY2027, 2026-08-26) put Agentforce ARR above $1.5bn, up over 240%, and AI plus Data 360 near $3.9bn — flattered by a wider definition from this quarter. Microsoft 365 Copilot went from 15m paid seats in January to about 30m by the June quarter, with net adds more than doubling. Against that: surveys of mid-market buyers describe 2026 as the year 2024-25 AI commitments meet real usage data, and only a minority report the returns they bought for. That is anecdote and forecast, which the sensor caps at watch, and no seller has reported a cancellation wave.
D4.source: Salesforce Q2 FY2027 results; Microsoft FY2026 Q3/Q4 calls; RBC CIO survey and renewal commentary (2026)

C5.value: vendors fund and guarantee their own buyers
C5.detail: The chip sellers have become lenders to the people who buy their chips. Nvidia is putting about $30bn into OpenAI and guaranteeing up to $105bn for an OpenAI-leased campus in Ohio (figures differ between reports), and in August set up a platform with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to raise more than $500bn for chip buyers, offering residual-value support of up to 25% per deal. AMD effectively guarantees a $300m Goldman loan to Crusoe that is secured on AMD chips. GPU-backed loans are now routine (CoreWeave $8.5bn in March, secured on chips plus a Meta contract). The buyer at the centre runs about $50bn of annual revenue against compute plans reported at $600bn to 2030, cut from about $1.4tn. Watch, not turning: no guarantee has been called and no vendor-financed buyer has missed a payment. The cut in OpenAI's plan is the thing to follow; a renegotiated contract with a vendor would be the turn.
C5.source: Yahoo Finance and The Conversation on Nvidia's OpenAI and Ohio commitments (Aug-Oct 2026); Nvidia financing platform announcement (August 2026); DCD on AMD and Crusoe; Bloomberg Law on CoreWeave's GPU loan; DCD on OpenAI's revised compute plan
